input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

input.section_summary: Motivate the challenge of reliable long-form scientific writing with large language models, state the research question—how does graph-guided sectioning affect coherence and citation quality?—and give a high-level overview of the graph-guided prompting workflow and conservative claim policy (always cite sources).

output:
Large pretrained language models offer new opportunities for drafting extended scientific text, but they also raise practical concerns about factual fidelity, citation consistency, and post-hoc auditability. (General background knowledge.) Motivated by these concerns, this work asks the following research question: how does an explicit, graph-guided approach to section planning and evidence injection affect local coherence and the fidelity of citations in automatically generated scientific sections?

To address this question we develop a graph-aware prompting workflow that treats the document as an explicit graph of interdependent sections and enforces strict, machine-checkable output formats. At a high level, the pipeline proceeds as follows:

- Construct a section graph that encodes parent/child relationships, precedence constraints, and citation dependencies for the target manuscript.
- Compute a leaf-first writing schedule that prioritizes sections with independently verifiable evidence.
- Retrieve and inject top-ranked evidence items for each scheduled section, preserving provenance metadata.
- Generate section drafts constrained to a JSON schema that requires explicit source pointers for all factual assertions and specified metadata fields.
- Validate, automatically repair when possible, and assemble validated section outputs into a LaTeX manuscript with a corresponding refs.bib that reflects the cited sources.

This paper adopts a conservative position on claims made by generated text: sections must provide explicit source citations for factual assertions, and the system exposes structured outputs to simplify human inspection and targeted edits. The principal contributions are (1) a graph-based section scheduler that operationalizes section dependencies and leaf-first generation, (2) an evidence-injection and prompt template protocol that couples retrieval results to constrained generation, and (3) an audit-friendly JSON output format and assembly procedure that integrate with standard LaTeX/bib workflows.

We evaluate the workflow by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, using metrics that prioritize citation coverage and unsupported-assertion rates; details of the datasets, metrics, and experimental protocol appear in Section 4, and quantitative and qualitative outcomes are reported in Section 5. We intentionally frame empirical claims conservatively and emphasize auditability: the system is designed to make both successful evidence integration and residual failure modes easy to inspect and correct.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 situates this work relative to prior approaches to long-form generation and citation-aware systems. Section 3 describes the graph construction, retrieval and ranking pipeline, JSON schema and validation rules, and the evidence-aware prompt templates in detail. Section 4 presents the experimental setup and evaluation protocol, Section 5 reports results and examples, Section 6 analyzes mechanisms and limitations, and Section 7 concludes with directions for future work.
